title: Mark Zuckerberg says the US should not block Chinese AI models
excerpt: Mark Zuckerberg has come out against one of Washington’s favourite ideas about artificial intelligence: that the way to beat China is to shut its models out. In an interview with the Financial Times published this week, Meta’s chief executive said banning advanced Chinese AI from use in the United States is “not an effective solution.” […]
content_html:
Mark Zuckerberg has come out against one of Washington’s favourite ideas about artificial intelligence: that the way to beat China is to shut its models out.

In an interview with the Financial Times published this week, Meta’s chief executive said banning advanced Chinese AI from use in the United States is “not an effective solution.”

His case is competitive rather than sentimental. Instead of building a wall, Zuckerberg argued, the US should work out where it is actually behind and fix those bottlenecks, a position that puts him alongside the startups urging Trump not to ban Chinese open-weight models.

He was not only talking about China. In the same breath he took aim at rivals closer to home, implicitly criticising OpenAI and Anthropic for pressing government to restrict powerful “frontier” models, an approach he cast as concentrating power in too few hands.

Openness, in his telling, is the natural direction of travel. “The big trend in the industry’s development has always been towards greater openness, putting technological power in the hands of more people, not fewer,” he told the paper.

There is an obvious tension in a Meta executive making this case. The company built its AI reputation on the open-weight Llama models, yet its newest flagship, Muse Spark, arrived closed source, a shift critics were quick to point out.

The timing is not accidental. His comments land in the middle of a live fight in Washington over whether to sanction or restrict Chinese AI, one in which Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has pushed back hard against the hawks.

The industry has split into camps. Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Elon Musk have lined up behind open weights, while OpenAI and Anthropic have argued for tighter controls on the most capable systems, on safety and national-security grounds.

That dividing line is partly about risk. OpenAI and Anthropic contend that the most capable models carry real dangers, from cyber-attacks to bioweapon uplift, and that unrestricted diffusion, including of Chinese open models, hands those capabilities to anyone who wants them.

Zuckerberg’s side sees the danger differently. In their view the greater threat is that a few American labs, and the government they lobby, end up controlling a technology that ought to be widely distributed, slowing innovation in the name of protecting it.

The backdrop to all of this is Chinese progress. A cheap Chinese model has been closing in on the American leaders, and the release of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 in mid-July sharpened the question of what, if anything, the US should do about it.

That question produced a letter. On 24 July, twenty-five organisations signed a document titled “Open Weights and American AI Leadership,” arguing that openness, not restriction, is the surer route to continued US primacy.

Zuckerberg’s own vision reaches past the immediate fight. He has described a future of “personalised superintelligence,” a system tailored to each individual rather than a single, centrally controlled model built to be safe on everyone’s behalf.

It is a framing that flatters Meta’s strategy as neatly as it challenges its rivals’. If the future is personal and open, the firms building closed, centralised systems are on the wrong side of history, and the ones giving models away are on the right one.

Washington does not have to accept that frame. Officials weighing export controls and model restrictions are balancing competitiveness against security, and Zuckerberg has now planted Meta firmly on the competitiveness side of the ledger.

What he has not resolved is the hardest part. Whether openness makes American AI stronger or merely easier to copy is precisely the judgement Washington is struggling to make, and one pointed interview will not make it for them.

content_html_zh:
马克·扎克伯格公开反对华盛顿最喜欢的人工智能观点之一：击败中国的方法就是将其模型拒之门外。

在本周发表的英国《金融时报》采访中，Meta 首席执行官表示，禁止中国先进人工智能在美国使用“不是一个有效的解决方案”。

他的案子是竞争性的，而不是感性的。 扎克伯格认为，美国不应该建造一堵墙，而应该找出自己真正落后的地方并解决这些瓶颈，这一立场使他与初创公司一起敦促特朗普不要禁止中国的开放重量模型。

他不仅在谈论中国。 与此同时，他把矛头指向了国内的竞争对手，含蓄地批评 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 向政府施压，限制强大的“前沿”模型，他认为这种做法将权力集中在太少的手中。

在他看来，开放是自然的旅行方向。 “行业发展的大趋势始终是更加开放，让更多人而不是更少的人掌握技术力量，”他告诉该报。

一位 Meta 高管在阐述这一观点时明显感到紧张。 该公司在开放重量的 Llama 模型上建立了人工智能声誉，但批评者很快指出，其最新旗舰产品 Muse Spark 是闭源的。

这个时机并非偶然。 他的言论正值华盛顿就是否制裁或限制中国人工智能展开激烈争论，英伟达的黄仁勋在这场争论中强烈反对鹰派。

该行业已分裂为两个阵营。 Meta、微软、英伟达和埃隆·马斯克都在支持开放权重，而 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 则主张以安全和国家安全为由，对最有能力的系统进行更严格的控制。

这条分界线部分与风险有关。 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 认为，最有能力的模型也带来了真正的危险，从网络攻击到生物武器升级，而不受限制的传播，包括中国的开放模型，将这些能力交给了任何想要它们的人。

扎克伯格一方对危险有不同的看法。 在他们看来，更大的威胁是一些美国实验室和他们游说的政府最终控制了一项本应广泛传播的技术，以保护技术的名义放慢了创新速度。

这一切的背景都是中国的进步。 一种廉价的中国模式已经逼近美国领导人，7 月中旬 Moonshot AI 的 Kimi K3 的发布加剧了一个问题：美国应该采取什么措施（如果有的话）。

这个问题产生了一封信。 7 月 24 日，25 个组织签署了一份题为“开放权重和美国人工智能领导力”的文件，认为开放而不是限制是美国继续保持领先地位的更可靠途径。

扎克伯格自己的愿景超越了眼前的战斗。 他描述了“个性化超级智能”的未来，这是一个为每个人量身定制的系统，而不是一个为了每个人的安全而构建的单一、集中控制的模型。

这个框架既赞扬了 Meta 的战略，又挑战了其竞争对手的战略。 如果未来是个性化和开放的，那么构建封闭、中心化系统的公司就站在历史的错误一边，而那些放弃模型的公司则站在正确的一边。

华盛顿不必接受这个框架。 权衡出口管制和模型限制的官员正在平衡竞争力与安全性，而扎克伯格现在已将 Meta 牢牢地置于分类帐的竞争力方面。

他没有解决的问题才是最难的。 开放性是否会让美国人工智能变得更强大，或者仅仅是更容易复制，这正是华盛顿正在努力做出的判断，一次尖锐的采访不会为他们做出这样的判断。
